title: Hand of Straights
description:
# Hand of Straights

Alice has a hand of cards. The value written on the `i`-th card is `hand[i]`, and duplicate values represent separate physical cards.

Rearrange every card into groups of exactly `groupSize` cards. Each group must contain `groupSize` consecutive integer values, such as `[4,5,6]` when `groupSize = 3`. The order of the groups does not matter, but every card must be used exactly once.

Return `true` if such a rearrangement is possible. Return `false` otherwise.

## Example 1:

**Input:** hand = [1,2,3,6,2,3,4,7,8], groupSize = 3
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** The cards can be rearranged as [1,2,3], [2,3,4], and [6,7,8].

## Example 2:

**Input:** hand = [1,2,3,4,5], groupSize = 4
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** Five cards cannot be partitioned into groups of four cards.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= hand.length <= 10^4`
*   `0 <= hand[i] <= 10^9`
*   `1 <= groupSize <= hand.length`

solutions.name: TreeMap Smallest-Card Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach
Count each card value in a `TreeMap`. While cards remain, the smallest remaining value must be the start of some group, so consume that value and the next `groupSize - 1` values one card at a time.

## Key Insight
The smallest unused card cannot be placed after any smaller value because no smaller value remains. Therefore it must open a consecutive group, and every required successor must be present immediately.

## Complexity Analysis
Each card is removed once, and ordered-map operations cost O(log n), so the total time complexity is O(n log n). The frequency map stores up to n distinct values, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Sorted Hand and HashMap Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach
Sort the hand, then count values in a hash map. Scan the sorted cards; whenever a card still has positive frequency, start a group there and decrement every consecutive value needed by that group.

## Key Insight
Sorting gives the same smallest-unused-card invariant without requiring an ordered map during removal. If an early remaining card is skipped as a start, no later card can cover it.

## Complexity Analysis
Sorting costs O(n log n), and the successful group decrements touch n cards in total, so the overall time complexity is O(n log n). The frequency table uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Open Groups Queue by Value Batches
solutions.description:
## Approach
Sort the cards and process equal values as one batch. Track how many consecutive groups are currently open and waiting for the next value. A queue records how many groups started at each distinct value so they can close after `groupSize` distinct steps.

## Key Insight
At value `x`, every open group must receive one `x`. If there is a gap while groups are open, or if the count of `x` is smaller than the number of open groups, the hand cannot be partitioned.

## Complexity Analysis
Sorting dominates the work at O(n log n). The batch scan and queue operations are linear, and the queue stores at most the number of distinct values, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: TreeMap Batch Frequency Subtraction
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use a `TreeMap`, but subtract groups in batches. If the smallest remaining card has frequency `k`, then `k` groups must start at that value. Subtract `k` from each of the next `groupSize` consecutive values.

## Key Insight
All copies of the current smallest value are forced to be group starts. Consuming them together exposes frequency deficits immediately and avoids repeating the same proof for identical cards.

## Complexity Analysis
Every distinct value is removed once and each ordered-map access costs O(log n), so for valid partitions the time complexity is O(n log n). The ordered frequency map uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Priority Queue of Unfinished Groups
solutions.description:
## Approach
Sort the hand and maintain unfinished groups in a priority queue ordered by their last card value. Each incoming card extends the group that currently ends earliest if it needs this card; otherwise it starts a new group.

## Key Insight
An unfinished group with the smallest ending value has the earliest deadline. If the current card is already larger than its required next value, that group can never be completed, so the answer is false.

## Complexity Analysis
Sorting costs O(n log n), and each card creates or updates one priority-queue entry in O(log n), so the time complexity is O(n log n). The queue can hold O(n) unfinished groups.
